citeAs: Goyal, N., Gao, C., Chaudhary, V., Chen, P.-J., Wenzek, G., Ju, D., Krishnan, S., Ranzato, M., Guzmán, F., and Fan, A. (2021). The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193.
creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan (Facebook AI Research)
description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage) and professionally translated into 101 languages. The dataset enables many-to-many multilingual translation evaluation across 10,100 language pairs, with all translations multilingually aligned and produced by professional translators through a carefully controlled quality assurance process.

rai:annotatorDemographics: The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators in the lab: 6 male and 4 female; with different roles (researchers including scientists and engineers, and program/project managers); originally from different regions: East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America. Professional translators and evaluators were employed through Language Service Providers; their specific demographics are not detailed.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed using a Translation Quality Score (0–100 scale) calculated per language based on identified errors by evaluation LSPs. All 101 languages in FLORES-101 met the acceptance threshold of 90% quality. About 50% of languages scored above 95%. Error categories were analyzed: the largest error category was mistranslation; register, grammar, and punctuation had few errors. Domain-level variation in error rates was observed within languages but no clear cross-language trend by domain was found.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Professional Language Service Providers (LSPs) — two translation LSPs and one independent quality assurance LSP
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Translations were produced by professional Language Service Providers (LSPs). The workflow involved: (1) translation by an initial LSP including internal editing; (2) automated quality checks (language identification, copy detection, length checks, fluency checks via language model, and detection of copying from commercial translation engines); (3) human quality assurance by an independent LSP using a Translation Quality Score (0–100 scale) based on error categories (grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, register) with severity levels (minor, major, critical); (4) re-translation if quality score fell below 90%. Two pilot experiments were conducted to select the best LSPs and determine the optimal workflow (A–C–A: same LSP handles translation and re-translation, independent LSP handles QA).
rai:dataBiases: All source sentences are in English, meaning non-English translations are produced by human translators and may exhibit translationese effects (overly literal or awkward translations). The authors acknowledge this but conjecture the effects are marginal for low-resource languages where MT systems produce many severe mistakes, and that the benefits of many-to-many evaluation outweigh the risk. Translators were explicitly prohibited from using commercial translation engines, and a heuristic was implemented to detect and reject translations that appeared to be copies from such engines, to avoid biasing reference-based automatic metrics.
rai:dataCollection: Sentences were sourced from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage). Articles were selected at random from each source, and 3–5 contiguous sentences were manually selected per article, avoiding very short or malformed sentences. One paragraph per document was selected from the beginning, middle, or end of the article (roughly one third each). The selected sentences were then professionally translated into 101 languages by Language Service Providers (LSPs) through a multi-stage workflow including translation, editing, automated quality checks, and human quality assurance by an independent LSP.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source sentences extracted from English Wikipedia, specifically from three Wikimedia sources: Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guide articles). A total of 3001 sentences from 842 articles were selected.
rai:dataLimitations: All source sentences are in English, so non-English translations may exhibit translationese effects. The test set is not publicly released but is available via an evaluation server to prevent overfitting. Several languages considered for inclusion were unable to meet the 90% quality threshold after multiple rounds of re-translation and were excluded. The dataset covers 101 languages, but many more languages exist that are not represented.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset is divided into three splits: dev (997 sentences from 281 articles), devtest (1012 sentences from 281 articles), and test (992 sentences from 280 articles). The test set is withheld from public release and is only accessible via an evaluation server to prevent overfitting.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Sentence selection avoided very short or malformed sentences. Paragraphs were selected from the beginning, middle, or end of articles with balanced distribution (roughly one third each). Sentences were manually labeled by sub-topic (one of 10 categories: crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, travel). Metadata including Wikipedia URL, topic, and boolean flags for hyperlinked entities and images were extracted for each sentence. Automated checks during translation included: language identification, copy-of-source detection, significant length difference detection, fluency check via language model, and detection of copying from commercial translation engines using a heuristic based on sentence-level spBLEU similarity.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to foster progress in machine translation for low-resource languages, which are spoken by the majority of the world's population. By providing high-quality evaluation benchmarks for 101 languages including many low-resource ones, the dataset aims to enable development of translation systems that benefit speakers of underrepresented languages. The authors hope it will support non-English-centric models that directly translate between languages such as African languages.
rai:dataUseCases: Primary use case is evaluation of machine translation systems, including many-to-many multilingual translation across 10,100 language pairs. Additional supported tasks include: document-level translation evaluation, multimodal translation evaluation (via image metadata), multilingual text classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automated quality checks during translation used: (1) a language identification tool; (2) a language model for fluency checking; (3) a heuristic based on sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU (spBLEU) to detect copying from commercial translation engines (comparing translations against outputs of commercial MT engines A and B). A SentencePiece tokenizer trained on monolingual data from all 101 languages was used for the spBLEU metric.

null_reasons.license: No license terms are explicitly stated in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a fixed number of independent annotations per item; translations went through multiple rounds but the number of independent annotations per sentence is not stated.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data in the collection process; languages that failed quality thresholds were excluded rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific start/end dates or collection period are stated in the paper, only average turnaround statistics (average 61 days per language, range 31–89 days).
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; languages failing quality checks were re-translated or excluded rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper mentions hope to expand language coverage in the future but does not describe a formal versioning or maintenance plan.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of translated Wikipedia sentences (news, travel, children's content) and does not contain personal or sensitive information.
